analysis.one_liner: Extends Do Not Call protections to cell phones and makes every illegal robocall worth at least $500 in court.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee; it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Do Not Call rules under federal law only cover residential phone lines, so calls to cell phones largely fall outside the registry. This bill would strike the word 'residential' from the law, covering all phone subscribers, and would let a caller be sued for any call to a number on the registry rather than only after repeated calls. It would also set $500 as the minimum, not the maximum, statutory damages per violation, and direct the FCC to rewrite its rules within 270 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Every phone subscriber whose number is on the Do Not Call registry, especially the growing share of Americans whose only phone is a cell phone. The bill gives them a private right of action for any call that violates the rules, with a $500 minimum per violation, which deters telemarketers and scam callers by making each unwanted call a lawsuit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone registered on the Do Not Call list

how_it_helps.text: Strikes 'residential' from section 227(c) of the Communications Act so the Do Not Call rules cover all telephone subscribers, not just landlines.
Removes the allowance for one call per entity per 12-month period to a registered number, making any violating call actionable.
Strikes 'up to' from the damages provision, making $500 the minimum statutory damages per violation rather than the maximum a court could award.
Directs the FCC to revise its Do Not Call regulations within 270 days of enactment to implement the changes.

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketers, robocall operations, and lead-generation callers who legally call numbers on the registry today, especially those calling cell phones, would face liability for every violating call plus a $500 minimum per call. Small businesses that telemarket would bear higher exposure, and defendants in TCPA suits would bear more litigation even when suits are weak.

drawbacks.text: Expanding the private right of action to any single call, with a $500 minimum per violation, could increase litigation exposure for small businesses that call a wrong number or operate call centers at scale, and could invite abusive TCPA lawsuits that banks, insurers, and debt collectors have long complained about.

Covering all subscribers, not just residential lines, means many routine informational calls and collections calls to cell phones would now count as violations, raising compliance costs that could be passed to customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change closing the cell-phone gap in the Do Not Call registry directly protects most Americans, since many have no landline and the registry does not cover them today. The private-right-of-action expansion is a real tradeoff: it deters scam callers but could also generate nuisance litigation against legitimate businesses, an objection the bill's sponsors did not address in the one-section text. On balance the protections outweigh the litigation risk, but the bill as written was brief and left compliance questions to the FCC.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or markup, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on March 20, 2024, with seven Democratic and two Independent cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telemarketers and robocall operations are better off, because they face no expanded liability, no coverage of cell phones, and no $500 minimum per violating call. Consumers keep getting calls to numbers they registered.

sides.party_line_note: All nine cosponsors were Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican signed on, and no recorded vote was ever taken to show broader support.

industries.note: The bill makes every call to a Do Not Call number actionable and sets a $500 minimum per violation, directly increasing the cost of high-volume calling, including calls to cell phones that are largely unregulated under current rules. Its industry interest runs against consumers who bear the calls.

Removing the one-call-per-year allowance means a single call to a registered number can support a lawsuit, so bulk call campaigns face statutory damages at scale rather than a de facto free first call.

industries.industry: Creditors, collectors, and banks that use outbound calling
industries.note: They would face higher litigation exposure from TCPA suits, including weak ones, which is a cost; but they also benefit from fewer scam calls eroding consumer trust in phone communication.
